groups.title: Linux File System & Navigation
groups.question: Explain how you find your way around a Linux server's files, and how you would dig through a large log file.

followUps.File System Hierarchy & Permissions: Your API can't read its config file. How do Linux permissions decide who can read it, and how do you fix it safely?
followUps.Pipes, Redirection & Text Processing: How would you count the 500 errors in a log file with one shell command, and what do the pipes do?

evidence.text: Each file has an owner, a group and everyone else, each with their own read, write and execute rights.
The API can read the file only if the user it runs as has read permission through one of those.
The fix is to give the service's user or group read access (chown/chmod), not to open it to everyone or run as root.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (chmod, chown, permissions) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Suggests chmod 777 or running the API as root as the fix.

evidence.text: A pipe sends one command's output straight into the next command's input.
You filter the matching lines (for example with grep) and count them (for example with wc -l) in one chained command.
Redirection sends output or errors to a file (>, >>, 2>) instead of the screen.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (pipe, grep, wc) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a pipe writes the output to a file on disk that the next command then opens.

groups.title: Process & Environment Management
groups.question: Explain how your API runs as a process on a server, and how it gets its configuration.

followUps.Processes, PIDs & Signals: What should your server do when it receives SIGTERM during a deploy, and what happens if it ignores it?
followUps.Environment Variables & .env Patterns: Why do secrets go in environment variables, and what goes wrong if a .env file is committed?

evidence.text: The server runs as an OS process with a PID that the system or platform can send signals to.
On SIGTERM it should stop accepting new requests, let in-flight ones finish, close connections and then exit.
If it ignores SIGTERM it gets killed forcefully after a timeout, dropping requests that were still in progress.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (PID, SIGTERM, signals) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says SIGTERM kills the process instantly and can't be handled.

evidence.text: Configuration and secrets are passed to the process from outside, not written into the code.
The same code runs with different values in development, staging and production.
A committed .env file puts the secrets into git history for anyone with repo access, so they have to be rotated.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (environment variables, .env) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says deleting the .env file in a later commit makes the leaked secrets safe again.

groups.title: SSH & Remote Access
groups.question: Explain how you log in to a remote server securely and keep long tasks running there.

followUps.SSH Key Pairs & Remote Login: Which key stays on your machine and which goes on the server, and why is that safer than a password?
followUps.tmux & Persistent Terminal Sessions: Your SSH connection drops during a migration. How does tmux keep it running?

evidence.text: The private key stays on your machine; only the public key goes on the server.
Logging in proves you hold the private key without sending it, so there is no password to guess or steal.
Private keys are never copied to servers or shared, and password login can be turned off.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (SSH, public key, private key) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the private key is the one placed on the server.

evidence.text: A process started in a plain SSH session is killed when the connection drops.
tmux keeps the session and its processes running on the server, independent of your connection.
You reconnect later and reattach to the same session to find the task still running.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (tmux, session) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says tmux keeps the SSH connection itself alive or reconnects it.

groups.title: Shell Scripting
groups.question: Explain how you would automate a repeated server task, like a nightly database backup.

followUps.Bash Variables, Conditionals & Loops: How does a bash script know a command failed, and how do you stop it from carrying on silently?
followUps.cron & Scheduled Jobs: How do you tell cron to run a job every day at 3am, and how would you notice if it stopped running?

evidence.text: Every command returns an exit code: 0 means success, anything else means failure.
The script checks it ($?, if, ||) or uses set -e so it stops at the first failure.
Options like set -o pipefail and set -u also catch failures inside pipes and unset variables.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (bash, set -e, exit code) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a command failed only if it printed an error message.

evidence.text: A cron line has minute, hour, day of month, month and weekday fields; 0 3 * * * runs every day at 3am.
cron gives no feedback by default, so a job that stops working goes unnoticed.
You notice failures by logging output, alerting on errors, or a check that the job actually ran (a heartbeat).

notEnough: Only naming the terms (cron, crontab) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says cron retries a failed job automatically.
